common loon <migrate@south.com> wrote:
:Reading the manifesto and the letters, it does become evident TK is
:nuts, but nuttiness does not invalidate the ideas in the manifesto any
:more than it invalidates the work of Ezra Pound, Edgar Allen Poe or any
:number of scientists/authors/artists.  As D.H. Lawrence said, "Trust the
:tale, not the teller."

I was really arguing against the proposition that TK's behavior was part
of some long-range, carefully thought out plan designed to publicize and
advance his anti-technology cause.  To me, TK's behavior is that of
someone with severe emotional problems and who just happens to like living
in the woods and tinkering with bombs.  That's not too much different from
your view of him, I think.  As for the validity of the ideas in the
Manifesto, that's another tale entirely, and a very long tale it would be
given the length of the Manifesto.  I'll leave a critical analysis of the
Manifesto to someone else -- someone with lots and lots of time on their
hands -- but I'll try and address some of your other points.

ON QUITTING BERKELEY
common loon wrote:
:I see one way you people go wrong.  You assume TK would be interested in
:a "career."  The problem is, many geniuses, particularly individualistic
:ones, do not think in terms of "career."  They devote their time to pure
:thought, rapt in the pleasure of abstract thought and the obsession to
:understand or create.   . . .

The factors that led TK to a career in mathematics are probably complex. 
He was certainly pushed by both parents into some sort of intellectual
career to the extent he really had no choice in the matter.  But he must
have found some things about mathematics and similar technical subjects
enjoyable.  I suspect that concentrating on such studies also allowed him
to temporarily escape from his personal problems the way others escape by
watching television and movies.  When he was a child studious behaviour
must have been strongly reinforced by his parents, so it is not surprising
that he continued to exhibit and apparently enjoy that type of behavior. 
In addition, he probably didn't see any more attractive alternatives to
the type of intellectual career he pursued.  

The strongest argument against the theory TK was primarily interested in
the pleasure of abstract thought is that he seems to have dropped
mathematics at the same time he abandoned his teaching career.  He
certainly could have continued his work in mathematics and even continued
to publish papers.  His area of research was not likely to be of any
practical use to technology. If this did worry him, he certainly could
have found areas of pure mathematics which will never be of any use to
anyone.  Instead, mathematical thought, when separated from his career,
was no longer attractive enough for him to pursue it further.

ON TACTICS
I wrote:
>2) If TK was interested in saving the environment and was able to cope
> with the emotional and social aspects of his teaching job at Berkeley,
> then why didn't he stay there?  Faculty positions at prominent
> universities -- and some not so prominent ones -- have provided many
> academics with convenient platforms from which they can express their
> opinions . . .

common loon wrote:
:Again, you presume life goals that have more to do with materialistic or
:social success than with ideology and conviction.  An ideologue with
:strong conviction in their beliefs, not to mention a preference for
:nature over "industrial society," would very likely do exactly what TK
:did.

As a tactic, quitting Berkeley was nutty.  If we can agree either that TK
is nuts or that he was simply escaping from a job he disliked, dropping
out of Berkeley is fully explained.  If his decision was driven by strong
convictions about the environment or technology, then we come back to my
first point. Where is the evidence he held these strong convictions
*before* quitting? 

On the other hand, if quitting was part of a long-range plan, then it was
a pretty bad one.  For example, consider whether entomologist Paul Erlich
could have more effectively advanced his notions about human population
control by adopting TK's method: an anonymous 18-year bombing campaign
followed by a rambling, poorly written Manifesto and a bunch of letters. 
As for the bombings themselves, let's be realistic.  One hundred times as
many bombs wouldn't have had much more effect on technology than to spur
the development of small portable x-ray scanners and explosive sniffers.
(All those new letter-opening jobs in mail rooms would cut down
unemployment a bit though.)

ON ENVIRONMENTALISM IN THE MANIFESTO

common loon wrote:
:There are references to the destruction of nature by the industrial
:system throughout the manifesto.  Here are the first two sentences: 
:"The Industrial Revolution and its consequences have been a disaster for
:the human race.  They have greatly increased the life-expectancy of
:those of us who live in "advanced" countries, but they have destabilized
:society, have made life unfulfilling, have subjected human beings to
:indignities, have led to widespread psychological suffering (in the
:Third World to physical suffering as well) and have inflicted severe
:damage on the natural world."  There is actually a lot about nature in
:the manifesto, but why focus on TK's motives, conscious or
:subconscious?  If he were just a bomber there would be no newsgroup
:devoted to him.  Is there a alt.fan.george.metesky or an
:alt.fan.guy.fawkes newsgroup?  

I've got to plead guilty to being much more interested in the
psychological aspects of the case than in any of TK's ideas.  I have read
the Manifesto and I was underwhelmed by TK's intellectualizing. 
Fortunately, you've picked two sentences that are pretty representative of
the Manifesto as a whole and bear out my contention that TK's primary
concern was not "protecting the environment."

"Inflicted severe damage on the natural world" is the only phrase in the
two sentences expressing concern for the environment and that phrase
appears at the end, almost as an afterthought.  Balance this against
"disaster for human race," "destabilized society," "made life
unfulfilling," "subjected human beings to indignites," and "led to
widespread psychological suffering" and you can see why I believe TK's
primary focus is the effect technology has on people (actually, just on TK
himself) while the environment is very much a secondary issue for him.  So
much so that his 1971 Essay doesn't have anything at all to say about
protecting the environment.

When TK does discuss nature in the Manifesto it is usually as a setting in
which people can be psychologically fulfilled and in which social
structures he believes desireable can exist.  This places man in a primary
position since it is man's needs which determine what should be done to
nature.  This is a rather different from the viewpoint of many
environmentalists that nature is primary and the effects of this policy on
man are of secondary importance.  

Overall TK's environmentalism seems to be that of the old-time hunters and
trappers.  We know he hunted elk -- successfully.  He routinely trapped
and shot small game for food.  Then there was that incident with the game
warden over TK's barbecued coyote.  There are suspicions he also poisoned
the deer that invaded his trunip patch.  Isn't this disturbing to some of
the environmentalists out there?  In fact, I continue to be puzzled as to
why we have heard so little criticism of TK from environmentalists.
